Notes

Hierarchy becomes physical: raised dogs, ancestors and forced bows establish a speaker who claims the right to control everything. Kitchen appliances and wordplay make the exaggerated cruelty grimly ordinary.

磕头

磕头 is the bodily act often called kowtowing: kneeling and bringing the forehead down. Here it is coerced submission, and later the demand continues until blood appears. Compare “Blessed,” where kneeling and joined palms ask for protection. The same lowered body expresses vulnerability there and an imposed hierarchy here, depending on who controls the gesture.

  • Lyric transcript (the passage discussed here)
祖宗

Claiming to be someone’s 祖宗, ancestor, is a way of asserting contemptuous superiority. 孙子, grandson, pushes the listener down the same hierarchy. The demanded 磕头 is a kneeling bow that brings the forehead to the ground, so the language of seniority becomes a physical demand for submission.

  • Chinese lyric transcript (Genius community)
亲手养大的狗

亲手 claims personal labor—“with my own hands”—and 养大 means raising something to adulthood. Calling the opponent a dog makes the care retrospectively into ownership: because I made you, you owe me obedience. This turns the mixtape’s recurrent worry about disloyal associates into an especially possessive account of the relationship.

  • Lyric transcript (the passage discussed here)
运球

运球 is the sporting action of moving with or dribbling a ball. Placed directly after stepping on someone’s head and before “life is like a game,” it lets humiliation slide into play. The sequence sustains control over the opponent while making the violence sound routine.

  • Chinese lyric transcript (Genius community)
我是个变态

变态 is a harsh label for someone warped or perverse. Here the speaker claims the insult himself and follows it with liking to get angry every day. That removes the expectation of proportionate behavior before the cooking threat arrives: the persona announces that excess is part of the performance rather than an accusation it will defend against.

  • Lyric transcript (the passage discussed here)
方太

方太 is Fotile, a kitchen-appliance company that makes range hoods. After the pressure-cooker threat, the very specific product detail makes the imagined kitchen mundane and recognizable.

  • Fotile: official kitchen-appliance catalog
焦油里掺了点焦虑

The sound runs from 交友 jiāoyǒu, making friends, to 焦油 jiāoyóu, tar, to 焦虑 jiāolǜ, anxiety. The first two are close in sound but very different in meaning; the shared 焦 keeps the chain moving. A literal English line preserves the bizarre mixture while this note restores the audible connection.

  • Chinese lyric transcript (Genius community)
哭

哭 kū, “cry,” and 酷 kù, “cool,” differ only in tone. The taunt turns the opponent’s crying into a question about their pose, closing the line with almost the sound it began with. The English captures the challenge but loses that tight sound reversal.

  • Chinese lyric transcript (Genius community)
祖坟冒青烟

祖坟冒青烟, blue smoke rising from ancestral graves, is a saying about extraordinary family good fortune or ancestral blessing. The second half takes the smoke literally and turns the auspicious expression into graves on fire. 燃起来 also works as “get fired up,” intensifying the collision.

  • People’s Daily: the ancestral-blessing expression in use
喊破喉咙

喊破喉咙 is to shout until the throat is ruined, a conventional way to say no amount of calling will help. The body echoes “Throat,” where the performer suffered while nobody cared. Here the arrangement reverses: the threatening voice imagines someone else exhausting their voice and declares in advance that it will not respond.

  • Lyric transcript (the passage discussed here)
你说要糖

Asking for candy infantilizes the opponent immediately after the demand for bloody submission. It suggests someone seeking a small soothing treat in a scene that offers none. The next line also refuses touch, so both comfort and access to the speaker’s body are withheld; the verse keeps all vulnerability on the other side.

  • Lyric transcript (the passage discussed here)
保险看心情开

保险 here is a gun’s safety catch. 看心情 makes a mechanism designed to prevent accidental firing depend on mood. The boast is therefore about unpredictability as much as firepower: the other person cannot count on a stable rule. That extends the earlier “I like getting angry” into the imagined weapon itself.

  • Lyric transcript (the passage discussed here)
太平间

太平间 is the ordinary word for a morgue, but its written parts contain 太平, peace or tranquillity. At the end of a line threatening incineration, that placid name lands with dark irony. The verse repeatedly puts violence inside familiar rooms and household vocabulary, from pressure cooker and range hood to this final place for the dead.

  • Lyric transcript (the passage discussed here)

About Jackzebra and this mixtape

Zhuang Zhuang Mixtape arrived on Surf Gang on October 2, 2026: 55 tracks, opening with Sour and closing with Sweet. Its cast widens from YoungQueenz on Poker Face to User116, Effie, kuru, yoyi, 春 and 南部犯罪份子. Aghast has a production credit on every track from Hitman through Snatch, giving that stretch a shared collaborator behind its changing scenes.

Surf Gang release · Artist credits

Jackzebra told AVYSS that he writes while singing over a beat he has listened to repeatedly, keeping the images in his head central. He values the room Mandarin leaves for indirect meanings. Listen for ordinary phrases becoming physical scenes: familiarity becomes cooking, authority becomes family seniority, and a tired saying suddenly turns into a threat.

AVYSS interview, 2024

In STATIC, he describes mixtapes as a format for letting ideas flow, reserving an official debut album for later. In a separate conversation about Above & Beyond, he compared that earlier tape to a collection of his producer friends’ work. The credits here likewise reward attention: long-running collaborators sit alongside guests working in Mandarin, Korean and English.

STATIC interview · Sabukaru interview, 2025

The small details connect to his stated interests: he has described playing Temple Run in transit and before shows, watching Top Boy, and wanting to score White Oleander. These give the songs specific points of contact with his life. The notes follow those connections alongside the lyrics’ jokes, invented scenes and competing voices.

His recommendations in Perfectly Imperfect · Dazed interview, 2025 · Interview questionnaire, 2025

Jackzebra has pushed back on being made to represent all of China’s underground. These notes stay close to the words: what an expression usually means, what changes in this line, and how another song answers it. Cultural references have sources; interpretations rest on details you can hear or read in the song.
